picks.title: When AI art has no author: Study finds generated images often can't be traced to training data
picks.excerpt: MIT researchers built a method that surgically removes individual training examples from a model and then measures what changes in its outputs. They find an 'attribution decay' effect: as datasets grow, deleting any single source image usually makes no measurable difference, so generated pictures often have no traceable ancestor.
picks.rationale: The first hard measurement of whether a generated image can be traced back to a specific source — it reframes credit, licensing and 'stolen style' arguments that designers are having every week.

picks.title: AI and 8 million digitized plant specimens reveal how the climate is changing nature in large parts of the world
picks.excerpt: Machine learning read flowering stages off eight million digitized herbarium sheets spanning a century, work contributed to by some 400 researchers in 40 countries. Global flowering times have shifted an average of 2.5 days per decade, with the sharpest moves in the tropics where rainfall patterns are breaking down.
picks.rationale: A century of pressed plants nobody could read at scale becomes a global climate signal — the clearest current example of AI turning dormant archives into new measurement.

picks.title: Seeing beyond BMI: Estimating cardiometabolic risk with smartphone imagery
picks.excerpt: Google Research introduced PhotoScan, a deep-learning system that estimates 3D body-composition metrics from ordinary 2D smartphone photos. It reaches near-clinical accuracy at predicting insulin resistance without DEXA or MRI hardware.
picks.rationale: Clinical-grade body composition from a phone camera collapses a hospital scan into an app screen — a concrete new sensing primitive for anyone designing health products.

picks.title: Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power
picks.excerpt: Penn State researchers paired synthetic DNA with a crystalline perovskite semiconductor to build a bio-hybrid memory element that stores more while drawing roughly 100x less power. The team frames it squarely at neuromorphic hardware: 'as the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a new strategy for low-power, high-storage devices.'
picks.rationale: A two-order-of-magnitude power drop from building memory out of DNA — evidence the answer to AI's energy curve keeps coming from new substrates, not bigger data centers.

picks.title: Organs age at different speeds: a blood test might soon tell which ones
picks.excerpt: CeMM trained deep-learning 'tissue clocks' on more than 25,000 histology samples to read biological age straight from tissue architecture, then linked those signatures to blood markers. 'Deep learning lets us read these spatial patterns, capturing aging as architectural remodeling,' the team reports in Nature Medicine.
picks.rationale: Aging measured as spatial structure a pathologist can't quantify by eye, then translated to a blood test — a Nature Medicine result that makes 'which organ is old' an answerable question.
